title: Disproportionate collapse made unavailable after loss of any one primary member

concept.text: The proposed innovation is an affordable structural system that confines collapse after the loss of any one primary load-bearing member to a declared local region. Within a specified class of buildings, loading conditions and construction tolerances, removing a column or a defined segment of bearing wall would not trigger collapse beyond that region. Local damage would remain possible; the intended advance is to prevent it from spreading through the structure.

The research objective is a simple structural mechanism or general design principle that gives the building this containment property without a separate project-specific study of every possible member-removal scenario. Existing performance-based approaches already pursue containment by assessing structural response to defined damage. The proposed advance would be a broadly justified system property covering every qualifying single-member loss within its declared scope. This is a proposed capability, not an achievement established by the supplied evidence.

significance.text: Disproportionate collapse occurs when local structural damage leads to a collapsed area much larger than the initiating damage would suggest. The supplied historical accounts connect robustness research and guidance to Ronan Point, the Murrah Building and NIST’s World Trade Center investigation. These examples motivate limiting failure propagation, although their initiating events and damage patterns differ and should not be treated as equivalent single-member losses.

Conditional assessment: if ordinary buildings could acquire reliable single-member collapse containment at ordinary construction cost, robustness could become an inherent property of the structural system. The direct consequence would be containment following a qualifying member loss. A sufficiently general, validated design principle could also substantially reduce reliance on individual removal-scenario studies, making this form of robustness easier to apply consistently. Those consequences depend on demonstrating coverage of the stated building class, loads, member locations and construction tolerances.

Protection against every blast or impact would not follow from single-member containment. One event can destroy several members, damage connections and impose additional loads; NIST’s account describes the Oklahoma City bombing as initially destroying three columns. Protection against an event would therefore be conditional on its damage and loading remaining within the system’s demonstrated envelope.

Scope synthesis: fire, foundation failure and simultaneous loss of multiple members remain separate challenges unless explicitly included in an expanded demonstration. Confining structural collapse would also not establish that the building remained undamaged, habitable or immediately usable. These limits preserve the distinction between preventing failure propagation and providing comprehensive protection from an extreme event.

missing_breakthrough.text: The sought breakthrough is a validated mechanism or structural argument connecting local member loss to a firm bound on subsequent collapse throughout a declared building class. The supplied accounts of ASCE/SEI 76-23 establish a mitigation framework involving performance objectives and assessment of defined damage. They do not establish the proposed ordinary-cost, any-member containment property, nor do they establish that no existing system possesses it.

Engineering synthesis: an alternate load path must remain usable after the original support disappears. Ties and catenary action—the ability of connected members to carry redistributed load through tension—are relevant mechanisms, but their presence alone does not establish containment. The design must account for the forces and deformations produced by sudden support loss, the strength and deformation capacity of connections, and the possibility that redistribution overloads adjacent members or connections. A general principle must explain why propagation stops, rather than simply identify another route for the load.

Proposed coverage challenges include corner-column removal, removal of defined bearing-wall segments, and member loss in a structure already affected by an earthquake. These cases challenge a design to work across different support geometries, structural systems and damage histories. They are useful targets for investigation, but the supplied evidence does not establish that all such configurations are comparatively unreliable or that existing approaches uniformly fail in them.

The earthquake interaction requires particular care. The available abstract of the December 2025 review identifies a gap in systematic treatment of earthquake-induced progressive collapse within standard seismic design procedures and examines whether special seismic detailing provides sufficient redundancy and integrity. The available material does not supply the detailed conclusions needed to assert that such detailing is generally inadequate.

Practical research requirements also remain to be defined: what counts as one wall segment, how far local collapse may extend, which construction errors are tolerated, and what additional cost qualifies as ordinary. A mechanism that works only with exceptional precision, extensive strengthening or unusually expensive connections would not meet the proposed affordability and ordinary-construction objective.

current_state.text: On June 5, 2023, NIST announced ASCE/SEI 76-23 as the first national building standard of its kind. Its stated purpose was to keep isolated structural failures from propagating into collapse of an entire building or a major part of it. NIST described a performance-based approach that sets structural goals while allowing designers to choose how to meet them. Its account also describes physical removal scenarios and experiments used to validate simulations, demonstrating an established research and assessment approach rather than a universal containment guarantee.

NIST described use of the standard as voluntary in June 2023. Engineering News-Record’s June 11, 2023 report stated that building-code use was not required and attributed to committee chair Donald Dusenberry the expectation that it would not become required. These are dated accounts, not verification of adoption in every jurisdiction or of adoption status on November 1, 2026. The standard itself was not retained in the supplied source collection, so this record does not claim an independent examination of its detailed provisions.

Mohammad Ashrafy and Reza Aghayari’s review, published December 18, 2025 in Bulletin of Earthquake Engineering, addresses progressive collapse of reinforced-concrete buildings during earthquakes. Its available abstract states that earthquake-induced progressive collapse has not been systematically included in standard seismic design procedures and says that the adequacy of special seismic detailing is critically evaluated. The retained material is a subscription preview. It supports that narrower account of the review’s scope and integration gap, but does not establish its detailed findings about the effectiveness of special detailing.

Evidence boundary: no prestressed-steel test evidence is supplied to substantiate the earlier assertion that corner-column removal remains a demonstrated weak case in those tests. The supplied material also contains no demonstrated ordinary-cost guarantee covering any single primary-member loss. Because the freshness record is empty, this establishes a limit of the available evidence, not proof that the capability remained unavailable throughout research and practice as of November 1, 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: test ordinary multi-story structures representing a declared building class, including a frame with a corner column and a bearing-wall building. Suddenly remove several different primary members under specified gravity loads and a stated lateral load. Define the permitted local collapse region before testing, including an explicit boundary for wall systems; one bay could be a proposed frame boundary where appropriate. Any collapse must remain within that region. These are proposed criteria, not established standards.
completion_criteria.label: Sudden primary-member removals confine collapse within predefined local regions

completion_criteria.text: Use independent specimens for different removal cases, or a protocol that explicitly measures and accounts for accumulated damage. Repeat the challenge with specified construction errors representative of ordinary practice. State the member locations, load levels, removal times, connection details, tolerances and measurement methods so that independent teams can reproduce the tests and assess whether containment depended on exceptional specimen quality.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible removal tests account for accumulated damage and construction errors

completion_criteria.text: A general any-member claim would additionally require a validated structural argument covering the declared building geometries, primary-member locations, connections, load combinations and construction tolerances. Experiments and validated simulations should challenge the assumptions and boundary cases of that argument. Finite tests establish demonstrated breadth; they do not establish literal universality. Tie-force calculations alone, or one successful column-removal test on a regular frame, would not satisfy this proposed evidentiary threshold.
completion_criteria.label: Validated structural argument covers any-member loss within the declared scope

completion_criteria.text: Practical acceptance would require a stated cost baseline and evidence that the system can be built using ordinary construction methods within the claimed cost range. The demonstration should identify the limits beyond which containment is unproven, including any exclusions for prior earthquake damage, fire, foundation failure or multiple-member loss. A successful result would support a bounded claim of collapse containment, without automatically establishing continued occupancy or repairability.
completion_criteria.label: Ordinary construction meets claimed costs with containment limits stated

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison: STR-07, “Topological control that denies an undesigned collapse mechanism,” has potentially substantial overlap with STR-12 because both concern preventing an unwanted structural failure mechanism. STR-12 specifies a trigger and outcome: loss of one primary member must not cause collapse beyond a declared local region. The supplied roster does not define STR-07’s mechanism or scope, so the earlier characterization of it as merely controlling a crack path in a brittle assembly cannot be retained as established. The entries remain distinct pending a fuller comparison.

Roster-based comparison: STR-10 concerns ordinary buildings remaining undamaged and usable after design-level earthquakes. STR-12 permits declared local damage and collapse while requiring containment after a qualifying member loss. STR-04’s seismic cloaking and STR-11’s passive damping address earthquake exposure or resonant response and could reduce demands that initiate damage. Their stated objectives do not, by themselves, demonstrate containment once a primary member has disappeared.

Roster-based comparison: STR-01’s flaw-tolerant, high-specific-strength members address material and member performance, while STR-03’s complete cast-mineral primary structure addresses what can constitute the load-bearing system. Either could supply components or a structural platform for STR-12, but member strength or material completeness alone does not establish building-wide load redistribution and collapse containment.

Roster-based comparison: STR-02’s autonomous restoration, STR-05’s reprogrammable mechanical state and STR-06’s growth and remodeling could intersect with adaptation or recovery after damage. STR-12 requires containment during the response to member loss, so later restoration would need a separate argument showing that propagation is arrested in time. STR-09’s validated lifespan law concerns prediction over service life, and STR-08’s structural energy storage adds another function to the primary structure; neither roster title establishes the single-member containment property.

Beyond the roster, robustness, alternate load paths, connection ductility and collapse isolation are relevant neighboring ideas. The supplied review mentions a 2024 paper titled “Arresting failure propagation in buildings through collapse isolation,” but supplies neither its contents nor a source URL. Its mechanism, demonstrated scope and implications for STR-12’s novelty therefore remain unresolved.

change_log.change: Preserved STR-12’s identity while defining the proposed any-member capability within explicit building, loading and construction-tolerance limits.
change_log.reason: The concept remains coherent, but the supplied evidence does not justify an unrestricted guarantee or establish that it has been achieved.

change_log.change: Dated voluntary-use and building-code statements to the June 2023 reporting.
change_log.reason: The sources establish historical statements and an attributed expectation, not adoption status through November 2026.

change_log.change: Replaced blanket blast and impact protection with containment following a qualifying single-member loss.
change_log.reason: A single event may damage multiple members; NIST’s Murrah Building account describes three initial column losses.

change_log.change: Identified the 2025 review’s authors and replaced the earlier quotation and detailing-failure assertion with the narrower available abstract findings.
change_log.reason: The supplied review identifies Mohammad Ashrafy and Reza Aghayari, while the subscription preview does not establish detailed conclusions about detailing effectiveness.

change_log.change: Retained corner, wall and combined earthquake/member-loss cases as proposed coverage challenges, and explicitly qualified the prestressed-steel test assertion.
change_log.reason: These are useful research targets, but the supplied evidence does not establish the claimed comparative weaknesses or provide the cited test results.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed demonstration to address wall boundaries, specimen reuse, construction errors, reproducibility, general structural coverage and cost.
change_log.reason: Finite removal tests need defined conditions and a validated argument to support a broader any-member claim.

change_log.change: Revised the STR-07 comparison using its supplied roster title and explained relevant distinctions across the other roster entries.
change_log.reason: The earlier crack-path characterization is not documented, and related objectives should not be merged with STR-12’s specific containment requirement.

change_log.change: Preserved source-access and freshness limitations without declaring the innovation false or absent.
change_log.reason: The standard was not captured, the 2025 review is available only as a preview, and retrieval dates do not establish a comprehensive current-state search.

unresolved_issues: Whether an existing structural system already provides the proposed ordinary-cost capability across a clearly defined building class is not established by the supplied evidence.
Building-code adoption and the research frontier through November 1, 2026 remain unverified because the supplied freshness record is empty.
The detailed provisions of ASCE/SEI 76-23 cannot be independently assessed from the supplied collection because the standard itself was not captured.
The 2025 review’s detailed conclusions about special seismic detailing and particular configurations remain unavailable in the retained subscription preview.
The earlier prestressed-steel corner-removal assertion requires identifiable test evidence; its absence here does not establish that the assertion is false.
The proposed building class, load envelope, wall-segment definition, permitted collapse region, construction-error range and affordability threshold remain to be specified.
STR-07’s full definition and the contents of the referenced 2024 collapse-isolation paper are needed to assess overlap and novelty.
